Brain–Computer Interfaces: The Chip Inside the Skull and the AI Outside It

A person with paralysis moves a cursor by thinking about moving their hand. A woman with ALS "speaks" at 62 words per minute through an implant. These are brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), and in 2025–26 they moved from a few lab demonstrations to dozens of implanted patients, a first market approval in China and a fast-growing industry. This explainer covers how they actually work: the electrodes, the tiny chip that has to fit inside strict heat and power limits, the AI that turns brain signals into words, the companies and trials, and the privacy questions they raise.

1. What a BCI is, and what it isn't

A brain–computer interface records electrical activity from the brain and translates it into an action: moving a cursor, selecting letters, producing text or synthetic speech, or controlling a robotic arm. Today's medical BCIs are built for people who have lost movement or speech through spinal-cord injury, stroke or ALS.

Two common misunderstandings are worth clearing up. First, current BCIs do not "read minds" in general: they decode specific, trained signals, mostly from the motor cortex, such as attempted hand movements or attempted speech. Second, a BCI is not a new kind of computer for AI. It is an input and output device. The implant's chip does very little computation; the AI that decodes the signals runs on ordinary phones, laptops or servers. That is why BCIs were not on the scorecard in Beyond Silicon: they use AI compute rather than add to it.

4. The chip's hard limits

The implanted chip is a tiny, extremely constrained computer. Its job is to amplify microvolt signals, digitise them, find the "spikes" (neurons firing), compress the data and send it out wirelessly, all while sealed inside the body.

  • Heat. Implant safety studies commonly use a limit of no more than 1 °C warming of surrounding tissue. In thermal simulations this allows only around 5 mW for a small 2 × 2 mm chip sitting in tissue, and roughly 70–75 mW for a larger unit mounted in the skull, where heat spreads more easily.
  • Data. Raw recording is a firehose: about 1,000 channels × 30,000 samples per second × 16 bits ≈ 480 Mbps. Detecting spikes and compressing on the chip brings that down to roughly 10–100 Mbps or much less ⚠️ secondary estimate. Transmitting raw data would cost too much power.
  • Power. Fully implanted devices recharge wirelessly through the skin by induction, which itself generates heat.
  • Longevity. The body attacks foreign objects; electrodes can be encapsulated by scar tissue and signals can degrade over years.

Heat and data budget simulator

Illustrative model. Power per channel and radio cost are assumptions chosen to be in a plausible range; the point is the trade-off, not exact numbers.

5. Worked example: Neuralink's N1

Neuralink's N1 is a coin-sized, fully implanted device that replaces a disc of skull. It records from 1,024 electrodes spread across 64 flexible threads, each thinner than a human hair and too fine to place by hand, so a surgical robot (R1) inserts them while avoiding blood vessels. Custom low-power chips in the implant process the signals before sending them wirelessly to an app; the battery is charged inductively.

Jan 2024 First human implant in the PRIME study.
Sep 2025 12 participants.
28 Jan 2026 "Two Years of Telepathy" update: 21 participants across trials; a speech-focused trial (VOICE) announced. Trials also run in Canada, the UK and the UAE ⚠️ secondary.
2026 Blindsight, a vision implant with an FDA Breakthrough Device designation (which speeds review; it is not an approval), had not been implanted in a person as of October 2026 per available reports.

6. The AI that decodes

The part of a BCI that has improved fastest is the software. Speech BCIs record from the parts of motor cortex that control the lips, tongue and larynx. A neural network maps each short window of neural activity to probabilities of phonemes (speech sounds); a language model then picks the most likely word sequence, correcting many errors, much as autocorrect does.

From noisy phonemes to words

Illustrative. Increase the decoder noise and see how much the language model recovers.

StudyParticipantResult
Willett et al., Nature 2023 (Stanford)Woman with ALS~62 words per minute; 9.1% word error on a 50-word vocabulary, 23.8% on 125,000 words
Card et al., NEJM 2024 (UC Davis)45-year-old man with ALS; 256 electrodes in 4 arrays99.6% accuracy on 50 words on day 1; 90.2% on 125,000 words on day 2; 97.5% sustained beyond 8 months; ~32 words per minute over 248+ hours of use
Kunz et al., Cell 2025 (Stanford/Emory)4 participants with ALS or strokeDecoded inner (imagined) speech with up to 74% accuracy; attempted and inner speech produce similar patterns
Meta, Nature 2025 (non-invasive)Thousands of volunteersWristband reading muscle signals (sEMG): handwriting at 20.9 words per minute with decoders that work across people without calibration
⚠️ The inner-speech finding cuts both ways Decoding imagined speech could help people who cannot even attempt to speak. It also means a device could pick up words a person did not intend to say. The researchers raised exactly this privacy concern and tested ways to keep the decoder locked until the user deliberately unlocks it.

8. Risks, ethics and law

  • Medical risk. Brain surgery carries infection and bleeding risk; endovascular devices trade some signal quality for avoiding open surgery.
  • Durability and abandonment. Electrodes degrade, and patients depend on companies for support; if a company fails, users can be left with unsupported implants.
  • Mental privacy. Neural data can reveal more than intended, as the inner-speech study showed.
  • Law. Colorado became the first US state to classify neural data as sensitive personal data (HB 24-1058, effective August 2024); California followed (AB 1008 and SB 1223, effective January 2025), and Montana in 2025. In November 2025 UNESCO adopted the first global Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology, which is not legally binding but calls for mental-privacy safeguards and freely given, informed consent.

9. What's next

Verdict BCIs are real, and for a small group of people with severe paralysis they are already life-changing: restoring typing, cursor control and speech at conversational speeds. The progress comes mostly from AI decoders and better electrodes; the implanted chip itself is deliberately minimal because heat and power limits are unforgiving. Broad consumer "brain chips" are not close. The next few years are about proving long-term safety, getting first approvals and reimbursement, and writing the rules for neural data before the technology outruns them.
